rules.statement: Never put a secret, token, authorization code or query string in an audit record or its details; record an identifier or a hash of the value instead.
rules.why: Audit records are persisted and indexed, so any secret they carry leaks into the store, the logs and the traces.
rules.check: Look at audit event properties and WriteAuditDetails implementations for client secrets, access/refresh/ID tokens, authorization codes, passwords or raw query strings being written.

rules.statement: When capturing the HTTP request context for an audit record, never include the query string, cut the User-Agent at 512 characters, and take the source address from Connection.RemoteIpAddress rather than parsing forwarding headers.
rules.why: The query string can carry codes or tokens, and the host has already corrected RemoteIpAddress for a trusted forwarding proxy.
rules.check: Look for Request.QueryString, Request.Query or the full URL in audit request capture, an untruncated User-Agent, or reading X-Forwarded-For directly.

rules.statement: Capture the audit request context when the event is published, not inside a sink or background handler that may run after the request has completed.
rules.why: Sinks run in the background after the request ends, when the HttpContext is no longer valid.
rules.check: Look for audit sinks or background handlers reading HttpContext or IHttpContextAccessor instead of the request context stored on the event.

rules.statement: Give an audit failure a required machine-readable error code (with optional message and status code), and don't add a free-text reason field to an audit event.
rules.why: Operators have to group failures by a code. Free text can't be filtered without parsing prose.
rules.check: Look for audit errors built without a code, or new event properties such as Reason or Description of type string used in place of an error code.

rules.statement: Have an audit event write its event-specific details through a typed method that takes a Utf8JsonWriter, never through an IDictionary<string, object> bag or a [JsonExtensionData] member.
rules.why: A dynamic bag lets any value, including a secret, reach the persisted record and invites magic-string keys. A typed writer stays reviewed and is trimming- and AOT-safe.
rules.check: Look for dictionary/object bags, [JsonExtensionData], or reflection-based serialization of audit event details.

rules.statement: Don't model an open set of event or record types as a closed polymorphic [JsonDerivedType] hierarchy listed on the base type.
rules.why: A package that adds an event would have to edit the library, which breaks the rule that vocabularies are open.
rules.check: Look for [JsonDerivedType] attributes listing every event subtype on an audit or event base type.

rules.statement: Use the audit record's field names, declared once in a constants class, for the log state keys, span tags and metric attributes, rather than inventing names or repeating string literals.
rules.why: One set of names lets an operator pivot from a record to its log entry, trace and metric. The log state isn't checked by a source generator, so the constants are the only guard.
rules.check: Look for audit log, span or metric keys written as inline string literals, or names that differ from the record's snake_case field names.

rules.statement: Limit audit metric attributes to bounded fields such as event name, category and outcome, and never tag metrics with subject, client, tenant or request identifiers.
rules.why: Metric dimensions must be bounded. The unbounded identifiers belong in the record, the log entry and the span.
rules.check: Look at metric tag lists in audit and telemetry code for ids, IP addresses, user agents or other unbounded values.

rules.statement: Don't report a direct ILogger.Log call in the audit logging handler as a breach of the [LoggerMessage]-only rule, but do require a // comment at the call that cites the decision allowing it.
rules.why: A source-generated logging method has a fixed parameter list, while the audit.* state keys vary for each event. That makes this a documented exception.
rules.check: Before flagging ILogger.Log, check whether it is the audit handler that logs flattened audit.* state. If it is, check only that the citing comment is present.

rules.statement: Log a structured audit record as flattened key/value state (objects dotted, numbers kept as numbers), not as a single JSON string property or a text template sentence.
rules.why: A collector can't index fields that are inside one opaque string or inside prose.
rules.check: Look for audit logging that passes the serialized record as one {Record} placeholder or renders the event into a message sentence.

rules.statement: Generate audit event ids with Guid.CreateVersion7 and write event times as UTC RFC 3339 with a Z suffix.
rules.why: Time-ordered UUIDv7 identifiers index and paginate well, and a UTC Z timestamp is unambiguous.
rules.check: Look for Guid.NewGuid for audit event ids, local times or offsets other than Z, or non-RFC 3339 formats.

rules.statement: Don't add a custom correlation id to an audit record. Use the W3C trace and span ids of the current Activity and HttpContext.TraceIdentifier as the request id.
rules.why: These identifiers let a record pivot straight to traces and to the host's HTTP logs.
rules.check: Look for new correlation-id fields, headers or generated ids in audit records instead of Activity.Current trace and span ids.

rules.statement: Keep one schema version for the whole audit record, bump its minor version when a field is added to a released schema, and give no individual event type a schema version of its own.
rules.why: A single record version gives consumers one thing to check, and per-event versions fragment the schema.
rules.check: Look for new envelope fields added without a schema version change, or SchemaVersion properties on individual event types.

rules.statement: Omit audit record members that have no value, including an empty resources array, rather than writing nulls or empty values.
rules.why: The record format leaves out absent members. Nulls and empty values add noise to the indexed store.
rules.check: Look for audit writer code that writes null values, empty strings or an empty resources array.

rules.statement: Compute an audit event's resources from its typed properties, listing the target first and then the entity that owns it, rather than having the recorder set them.
rules.why: Deriving resources from typed properties keeps every acted-on entity in the record consistently, and the order states the ownership.
rules.check: Look for recorder code that assigns resources by hand, or resource lists where the owning entity comes before the target.

rules.statement: State the actor type explicitly for each audit recorder method, and derive the log level from the event's severity (info is Information, warning is Warning, critical is Critical).
rules.why: The caller has to be stated in the record, not implied by the event type, and the log level must match the severity an operator alerts on.
rules.check: Look for new recorder methods that don't set an actor type, or audit log levels chosen independently of severity.

rules.statement: Write a JSON record into a pooled buffer writer without allocating a byte[], and read it back with JsonElement.Parse rather than JsonDocument.
rules.why: Binary data uses pooled rentals and allocates no byte[]. JsonElement.Parse avoids a disposable document.
rules.check: Look for ToArray(), new byte[] or MemoryStream in record serialization, or JsonDocument.Parse used to read a record back.

rules.statement: Add a matching entry to the audit-records event catalog document when an audit event is added or renamed.
rules.why: Adding or renaming an event is a reviewed change to the catalog that operators rely on.
rules.check: Look for a new or renamed audit event name constant without a matching change to the audit-records documentation.
